Hi Heloise

I came across in similar problem with scr model. I think the initial value [inits()]. Yesterday, where I change the inits value of sigma (in my case with JAGS) the problem gone, but you might need to try several value.

BTW, how are you?

Best,

Soy

From: hmec...@googlegroups.com [mailto:hmec...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Helo?se Pavanato
Sent: Thursday, June 30, 2016 8:22 PM
To: hmec...@googlegroups.com
Subject: double-observer and repeated counts - dmulti

Dear all,

I am implementing a kind of N-mixture model with three parts:

1- multinomial model for double-observer data to estimate detection probability;

2- binomial model for replicate days (J=2);

3- Poisson model for abundance;

Nevertheless, I do not have a complete dataset: ng.cor (matrix of number of groups detected only by observer 1, only by observer 2 and by both observers) is partly completed and partly missed because I was only able to implement double-platform in two from five months.

Thus, in the cases where ng.cor[,1:3] is complete I use dmulti, and in the cases where ng.cor[,1:3] is not complete I just use a binomial distribution. That is why you will see four loops (two for each replicate - day) instead of only one.

When running this model I am getting the error regarding ng.cor2[1, 1:3]: "node inconsistent with parents".

I have already tried to change trials ngroups2 (to ngroups2 + 2 and + 5 and so on) and also N.compl (binomial model) and Ng (Poisson model).

Code are below and data can be downloaded here (Dropbox link):

https://www.dropbox.com/sh/1p9fidw1g4x702f/AACgJuaLuIg6IvbR_Klqjt9Ca?dl=0

I appreciate any suggestion.

Thank you a lot.

Best,

Heloise

#--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Density and abundance estimate from repeated counts

#--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Entry for Jags

load('dataC.inia.rda')

dimnames(dataC.inia)

str(dataC.inia)

load('rep1C.rda')

dimnames(rep1C)

str(rep1C)

load('rep2C.rda')

dimnames(comb_rep2C)

str(comb_rep2C)

# Number of detection per obs (front=obs1, back=obs2) and replicate

n1 <- data.frame(rep1C$replicate, rep1C$ngroups.obs1, rep1C$ngroups.obs2, rep1C$ngroups.both, NA)

n2 <- data.frame(comb_rep2C$replicate, comb_rep2C$ngroups.obs1, comb_rep2C$ngroups.obs2, comb_rep2C$ngroups.both, NA)

names(n1) <- c('rep', 'obs1', 'obs2', 'both', 'nd')

names(n2) <- c('rep', 'obs1', 'obs2', 'both', 'nd')

# To separate only samples with detections by front and back platforms (obs1 and 2, feb and jun)

# f1.cor and f2.cor are indexes that represent only double-platform data for day (k) 1 and 2.

# f1.on and f2.on are indexes that represent only sightings of observer 1 (front platform).

# The final object is a data.frame

i1 <- 1:nrow(n1)

f1c <- i1[n1$both >= 0]

f1.cor <- as.numeric(na.omit(f1c))

f1.on <- as.numeric(attributes(na.omit(f1c))$na.action)

i2 <- 1:nrow(n2)

f2c <- i2[n2$both >= 0]

f2.cor <- as.numeric(na.omit(f2c))

f2.on <- as.numeric(na.omit(i2[n2$obs1 >= 0 & is.na <http://is.na>(n2$both) == TRUE]))

# Initializing ngroups replicates and N

ngroups1 <- as.numeric(apply(n1, 1, max, na.rm = T))

ngroups2 <- as.numeric(apply(n2, 1, max, na.rm = T))

ngroups <- data.matrix(cbind(ngroups1, ngroups2))

ngroups.cor <- apply(ngroups, 1, max, na.rm = T)

N.compl <- cbind(ngroups1 + 2, ngroups2 + 2) # max from n1 and n2 + 2

# (jags does not accept data.frames as initial values)

# Data list for jags

ng.cor1 <- as.matrix(n1[f1.cor, 2:5])

ng.cor2 <- as.matrix(n2[f2.cor, 2:5])

ng1 <- n1[f1.on, 2]

ng2 <- n2[f2.on, 2]

data.list <- list(T = nrow(n1),

                  K = 2,

                  F1 = length(f1.cor),

                  J1 = length(f1.on),

                  F2 = length(f2.cor),

                  J2 = length(f2.on),

                  ng.cor1 = ng.cor1,

                  ng1 = ng1,

                  ng.cor2 = ng.cor2,

                  ng2 = ng2,

                  f1.cor = f1.cor,

                  f1.on = f1.on,

                  f2.cor = f2.cor,

                  f2.on = f2.on)

                  #rstate = cbind(rep1C$rstate + 1, comb_rep2C$rstate + 1),

                  #rain = cbind(rep1C$rain, comb_rep2C$rain),

                  #effort = cbind(rep1C$effort, comb_rep2C$effort))

# Parameters to be monitored

params <- c('p1', 'p2', 'pd', 'p.em', 'lambda', 'Ng')#, 'a0', 'a1', 'a2')

# MCMC inits

inits <- function(){ list(p1 = runif(1), p2 = runif(1),

                          ngroups1 = ngroups1[f1.cor], ngroups2 = ngroups2[f2.cor],

                          N.compl = N.compl,

                          #a0 = runif(1), a1 = runif(1), xrs = c(0.1,0.1,0.1),

                          #a2 = runif(2), xr = c(0.1,0.1), sigma = runif(1), mu.e = runif(1),

                          p.em = runif(1),

                          lambda = rpois(1, 4),

                          Ng = ngroups.cor + 5

                          )}

#--------------

# Model in BUGS

#--------------

sink('riverdolphin.do.txt')

cat('model {

## Priors:

  p1 ~ dunif(0,1)

  p2 ~ dunif(0,1)

  #a0 ~ dnorm(0,0.01)

  #a1 ~ dnorm(0,0.01)

  #for(i in 1:3){

  # xrs[i] ~ dunif(0,1)

 #}

  #for(i in 1:2){

  # a2[i] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)

   #xr[i] ~ dunif(0,1)

 #}

  #mu.e ~ dnorm(10, 0.1)

  #sigma ~ dunif(0,20)

  #tau.e <- 1/(sigma*sigma)

  p.em ~ dunif(0,1)

  lambda ~ dunif(0,500)

## Likelihood:

## Observational process

        p[1] <- p1 * (1 - p2) # detected only by obs1

        p[2] <- (1 - p1) * p2 # detected only by obs2

        p[3] <- p1 * p2 # detected by both

        p[4] <- 1 - (p[1] + p[2] + p[3]) # non-detection probability

        pd <- 1 - p[4] # detection probability

        # multivariate probability vector for transect i (only for Feb and Jun)

        pdc[1] <- p[1] / pd

        pdc[2] <- p[2] / pd

        pdc[3] <- p[3] / pd

 for(f1 in 1:F1){ # F1: number of transects with double-platform day 1

        # f1.cor is the index of transects with double-platform (i.e., without NAs)

        ng.cor1[f1,1:3] ~ dmulti(pdc[1:3], ngroups1[f1])

        ngroups1[f1] ~ dbin(pd, N.compl[f1.cor[f1],1])

 } # f1

 for(j1 in 1:J1){ # J1: number of transects with only one observer day 1

        # f1 is the index of transects with only one observer

        ng1[j1] ~ dbin(p[1], N.compl[f1.on[j1],1])

 } # j1

  for(f2 in 1:F2){ # F2: number of transects with double-platform day 2

        # f1.cor is the index of transects with double-platform (i.e., without NAs)

        ng.cor2[f2,1:3] ~ dmulti(pdc[1:3], ngroups2[f2])

        ngroups2[f2] ~ dbin(pd, N.compl[f2.cor[f2],2])

 } # f2

 for(j2 in 1:J2){ # J2: number of transects with only one observer day 2

        # f2 is the index of transects with only one observer

        ng2[j2] ~ dbin(p[1], N.compl[f2.on[j2],2])

 } # j2

## Density process

# Emigration rate

 for(i in 1:T){ # T: number of transects

    for(k in 1:K){ # K: number of replicates (days)

        # p.em is the emigration probability

        # N.compl is the total population that uses the area

        N.compl[i,k] ~ dbin(p.em, Ng[i])

       # logit(p.em[i,k]) <- a0 + effort[i,k] + a1*rstate[i,k] + a2[rain[i,k]]

       # effort[i,k] ~ dnorm(mu.e, tau.e)

       # rstate[i,k] ~ dcat(xrs[])

       # rain[i,k] ~ dcat(xr[])

    } # k

# Groups density

        # NG is estimated for all transects (f1.cor + f1.on) and (f2.cor + f2.on)

        Ng[i] ~ dpois(lambda)

 } # i

# Mean of parameters

   #p.em.m <- mean(p.em[,])

}

')

sink()

#-----------

# Fit model

#-----------

library(jagsUI)

fit.do <- jags(data.list, inits, params, 'riverdolphin.do.txt', n.chains = 3,

          n.thin = 500, n.iter = 100000, n.burnin = 60000, parallel = T)

print(fit.do, dig = 3)

plot(fit.do)

#save(fit.do, file = 'fit.do.rda')

messages.subject: Shouldn't posterior predictive checks be computed from lambda[i] instead of N[i]?
messages.subject_clean: Shouldn't posterior predictive checks be computed from lambda[i] instead of N[i]?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been using the chi square based posterior predictive checks as described in BPA and in AHM1
chapter 6.8 for some time already. Now I'm testing goodness of fit of my N-mix models
(both unmarked::pcount and equivalent JAGS model). I also tried Nmix.gof.test(),
which is similarly based on chi square. I noticed there is a big difference in both stats,
Nmix.gof.test() giving much higher values (~ 500) than PPC in JAGS (~ 75).

After some examination I found the reason. The Nmix.gof.test() is based on
lambda:

sum((Y[i,j]-lambda[i,j]*p[i,j])^2/(lambda[i,j]*p[i,j]))

whereas the PPC is based on N:

sum((Y[i,j] - N[i]*p[i,j])^2/(N[i]*p[i,j] + constant))

The extra constant is not what makes the huge difference; it is the N versus
lambda. Because the N[i] in the JAGS model already reflects the values
Y[i,j]! In my case, the lambda[1] = 4.47, Y[1,] = c(12, 11, 12), and the
N[1] posterior distribution doesn't go below 12 even if the lambda is much lower!
So this is the reason why the PPC chi square is much lower - because the
"expected" (fitted) values of N*p already accomodate to observed values Y so
that N is never smaller than Y even if lambda is.

I just wonder whether we shouldn't use lambda[i] instead of N[i] for PPC
checks as well. My ideas behind this:

1) the idea of the "fitted" part of the formula is that this should be the
prediction of the model. And the prediction of the model shouldn't be
affected by the actual value of the observation. In the formula:

Y[i,j] - N[i]*p[i,j]

the N[i] is directly affected by Y[i,j], which seems to violate the purpose
of this test, which is to compare predictions *without* knowing particular
Y with that particular value of Y.

2) now it is inconsistent in how we test models in unmarked and in
bugs.

What do you think?

Best regards,

	Tomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

I would say that a fit statistic or discrepancy measure can be calculated in a number of different ways and what matters is the relative comparison between the realizations of the model (i.e., observed vs. simulated data).  The question you are describing is whether fit should be assessed by the realized (N) vs. expected (lambda) abundances.  But again, as long as the comparison is consistent within the check between observed and simulated data, I think the conclusions would be the same.

What are your objectives regarding the use of both an unmarked and a JAGS model?  Another thing to consider is the conceptual difference between how GOF is assessed using parametric bootstrapping vs. posterior predictive checks.  The former does not incorporate parameter uncertainty, as each replicate data set is simulated from the same model fitted to the observed data.  I bet if you fit the posterior predictive check using lambda instead of N, the discrepancy values would be higher for JAGS.  Of course, you can't easily fit the parametric bootstrap to N for the unmarked model since the latent abundance does not exist in the same sense.

Either way, these goodness-of-fit assessments are just a general way to diagnose problems and are not well understood.

messages.subject: Camera traps: false-positives and gregarious species
messages.subject_clean: Camera traps: false-positives and gregarious species
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have count data from camera traps (210 sites, 25 occasions at each), and would like some advice on approaches to model abundance of solitary (e.g. Agouti) and gregarious (e.g. White-lipped Peccary) unmarked species, for whom is it not possible to diferentiate individuals at the same site and occasion.
Since camera trap effective sampled area is around 20 m x 6 m plot (the area in front of camera at which sensor can detect some animal), and it is a small area considering species' home ranges and daily movements,
to adopt a Temporary Emigration N-mix model (Chandler at al., Ecology 92(7) 2011, gpcount in unmarked) sounds important.

In Marc and Royle's AHME book, they suggest the use of N-mix Poisson/Poisson for solitary species with probable many false-positives
on counts at the same site and occasion (the same individual recorded many times). Should the use of a Poisson distribution for counts in a model aslo considering Temporary Emigration (instead of a Binomial, as in gpcount) be the best option for these species?

For gregarious species, AHME book suggest the choice of a beta-binomial underlying the count in N-mix model. To apply a beta-bionmial in a Temp Emig N-mix model would be the best option?
For each independent group record we have the minimum number of different individuals of the group, and maybe group size could be modeled considering spatial covariates. Is there such approach for N-mix models?

Thanks for any comment!

Cheers,

Igor

messages.subject: Re: convergence - HDS
messages.body_plain:
The PSRF is the same as r-hat (with MPSRF equivalent to the multivariate r-hat), so I'm not sure that this will provide different information. I think of the Raftery as being useful for figuring out how long to run a single chain in order to achieve a certain level of accuracy, but I'm not sure there's any formal way to convert the dependence value for a single chain into a requisite length for multiple chains (but curious to hear if there is!).  The Geweke is designed to find the non-stationarity displayed in Marc's post. My extremely speculative guess is that your chains are converging, but the burn-in could run a little longer.  If you chop out some of the initial saved iterations, does the Geweke change at all?

John

messages.subject: binomial-binomial hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to write a model where the state and the observation process are both binomials. The state process is survival within a group when group size prior to survival is known. The second binomial is an observation process and occurs after the survival process. There is one binary covariate for survival, like habitat type (A or B) and there are no covariates for detection. I simulated a data set where survival in habitat A is  0.6, survival in habitat B is 0.75 and detection is 0.6. There are two observations per group.

I keep running into trouble though, in that survival in one of the groups always seems to always get stuck at 1 periodically and it throws off the estimates of my other parameters. Is there something fundamentally improper about formulating a model this way (two binomials), or am I missing something obvious? It does seem to be sensitive to the precision of my uninformative priors (i.e. parameter ~dnorm(0, < 0.001) gives wonky results).

I'm just looking for feedback on if I am missing something simple. I can share my data simulating code and the model for R2OpenBUGS if needed.

Thanks!

-Tim

messages.body_plain:
Hey Tim, the problem might have to do with the normal prior on the logit-scale probability.  For intercepts, this prior can be problematic because it causes a bathtub shape on the probability scale:

hist(rnorm(1000,0,sqrt(1/0.001)))
hist(plogis(rnorm(1000,0,sqrt(1/0.001))))

Better to set a uniform prior on the probability scale before transforming to logit scale.  Or you could trick the normal prior with a tau value of 0.37, which approximates a uniform when transformed:

hist(plogis(rnorm(1000,0,sqrt(1/0.37))))
